title: Why should objects be immutable, and when should you make them so?
summary: The trade-off it's testing you can articulate, not the claim that immutability is always better.

slides.markdown:
"Immutability is good" is a slogan every candidate has heard. This question tests whether you can go one level deeper: name the concrete benefits, name the real cost, and name a case where it genuinely isn't worth it.

A candidate who treats immutability as a universal good, with no cost, hasn't actually thought about the trade-off — they've memorized the conclusion of someone else's trade-off.

Ask: **"Immutability of what, specifically — a small value object, a config object, or a whole domain model?"** The answer genuinely differs by scope. A small value object (a `Money`, a `Point`) is almost always worth making immutable — the cost is trivial. A large, frequently-updated domain entity is a much harder call, where the copying cost and API awkwardness can be real.

This question lets you scope your answer instead of giving one blanket verdict for every kind of object.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: benefits, cost, and when it's not worth it
slides.markdown:
Three moves: **name the benefits** (thread safety without locks, safe to share and cache, easier to reason about since state never changes underneath you), **name the cost** (every "update" allocates a new object, more garbage for the collector, sometimes more verbose call sites), then **name when it's not worth it** (a large, hot-path object updated thousands of times per second, where allocation pressure genuinely matters).

See [immutability-as-a-design-tool](immutability-as-a-design-tool) for the deeper treatment this answer draws from.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a mutable class refactored to immutable

slides.markdown:
| | Immutable | Mutable |
|---|---|---|
| Thread safety | Safe to share across threads with no locking | Needs synchronization or defensive copying |
| GC pressure | An "update" allocates a new object every time | Updates reuse the same memory, less garbage |
| Ergonomics | Builders/wither methods can feel verbose | Simple setters, familiar and terse |
| Reasoning | State never changes underneath you — easier to trust | Must track every place that could mutate it |

**How to decide:** if the object is shared across threads or cached, immutability's safety usually outweighs its allocation cost; if it's a large object mutated at very high frequency on a single thread, mutability can be the pragmatic choice.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a wither method instead of mutating in place
Follow-up: how do you 'update' an immutable object efficiently?
slides.markdown:
Two common patterns. **Wither methods** (as above) return a new instance with one field changed, reusing the unchanged fields by reference rather than deep-copying them — cheap when most of the object's data is shared, not duplicated. **Copy-on-write** collections take this further at the data-structure level: a persistent list or map shares most of its internal structure between the old and new versions, so an "update" is closer to O(log n) than a full O(n) copy.

The practical takeaway: "immutable" doesn't have to mean "copy everything every time" — smart sharing of unchanged parts keeps the allocation cost far lower than it looks at first glance.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: is immutability enough for thread safety?
slides.markdown:
Not entirely on its own — it removes the biggest category of thread-safety bugs (races on mutable shared state), but a class only counts as truly immutable if every field is both `final` **and** itself immutable or defensively copied. A `final List<String> items` field is still a trap if the constructor stores the caller's actual list reference — the caller can mutate it after the fact, and now your "immutable" object's contents just changed.

See [thread-safety-fundamentals-for-objects](thread-safety-fundamentals-for-objects) for what else complements immutability once state genuinely needs to change under concurrency.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: what's the memory/GC cost story at scale?
slides.markdown:
On a genuinely hot path — millions of updates per second to a large object — immutability's "allocate a new object per update" model can create real garbage-collection pressure: more short-lived allocations mean more minor GC cycles, and if the objects are large enough or long-lived enough, more work for the collector overall.

The honest answer isn't "never use immutability at scale" — it's "measure it." Modern generational garbage collectors are tuned for exactly this allocate-and-discard pattern, and it's often cheaper than expected; the point of naming the cost is to show you'd verify it with profiling rather than assuming either extreme.

**Weak answer:** "Immutable objects are always better — you should make everything immutable."

**Why it's weak:** it names zero cost, which means it isn't a design judgment, it's a slogan. Every object has some genuine cost to making it immutable — allocation, verbosity, sometimes real GC pressure at scale — and pretending otherwise is the tell that you haven't actually weighed the trade-off.

**Correct model:** name the specific benefit you're buying and the specific cost you're paying for *this* object, in *this* context.

slides.sectionTitle: Wrong answer: calling a class immutable when it isn't
slides.markdown:
**Wrong answer:** "This class is immutable — all its fields are `final`." ...while one of those `final` fields is a mutable `List` that callers can still reach into and modify.

**Why it's wrong:** `final` only prevents *reassigning* the field, not mutating the object it points to. A `final List<String> items` field still lets any caller with a reference call `items.add(...)` and change the object's actual contents — the class only *looks* immutable from its field declarations.

**Correct model:** true immutability requires defensively copying (or wrapping as unmodifiable) any mutable field on the way in and out, not just declaring the reference `final`.

"Immutable objects are safe to share across threads with no locking, safe to cache, and easier to reason about since their state never changes underneath you. The cost is that every 'update' allocates a new object — more garbage for the collector, sometimes more verbose call sites via builders or wither methods. I'd reach for immutability by default for small value objects and anything shared across threads, and reconsider it only for a large object mutated at very high frequency where allocation pressure is a measured, real problem — not an assumed one."
